title: Listening counts too
hookLine: the tradition forbids listening to gossip, not only speaking it

lines: THE EAR IS NOT A BYSTANDER.
cards: Gossip is a two-person job. One to say it, and one to lean in. Someone lowers their voice: okay, don't repeat this.
The listener's face does half the work: eyebrows up, chair pulled closer, tell me everything. Without that face, gossip can die in the first sentence. All week the focus has been on the mouth.
Jewish teaching on speech doesn't let the ear off the hook as an innocent bystander.

teach.h: DON'T SPREAD IT, DON'T TAKE IT IN.
teach.b: Listening counts too. Turn it four ways. First, the verse.

In Exodus, among the laws for honest courts: "Thou shalt not utter a false report." The rabbis of the Talmud read that line in two directions at once: don't spread a false report, and don't take one in.
The verse that guards the mouth guards the ear. Second, the body.
The Talmud, in tractate Ketubot, asks a playful question: why are human fingers shaped like pegs? So that if a person hears something unfit, they can put their fingers in their ears.
And why is the ear hard but the earlobe soft? So the lobe can be folded in to close it. Half a smile and half serious: the ear can close, and knowing it can is the point.
Third, what not listening looks like. It's rarely a speech.

teach.h: CHANGE THE SUBJECT, OR DOUBT IT.
teach.b: Changing the subject. Asking, should we be talking about this? Finding a reason to refill the coffee.
And if the words have already landed, the teachers of speech, the Chafetz Chaim among them, ask the listener at least not to believe it, to hold it as unproven rather than true.
Fourth, the stretch behind you: responsibility, then lashon hara, the Chafetz Chaim, rechilut, motzi shem ra, feathers that can't be gathered.
Each piece closes a door, and the ear closes the last one: gossip with nobody to hear it has nowhere to go.

how: Jewish laws of speech, as the Chafetz Chaim sets them out, treat listening to and believing lashon hara as forbidden alongside speaking it; observant Jews try to change the subject or leave when gossip starts.

o: hearing gossip is part of the harm too
listening well is the best kind of kindness
only the speaker is to blame for gossip

games.q: listening counts too — tap the pairs.
p: don't spread it, don't take it in
so the ears can be closed
change the subject or step away

s: only the person who speaks gossip does wrong
the rabbis read Exodus as forbidding taking in a false report, not only spreading it.
the Talmud says the body is built to stop listening
Ketubot: fingers shaped like pegs and a soft earlobe, so the ear can close.
refusing gossip means lecturing the speaker
the exits in the lesson are quiet ones: change the subject, step away, or decline to believe it.

games.q: a friend leans in: "okay, don't repeat this, but..." about someone you both know. what do you do?
o: lean in; you won't repeat it, so it's harmless.
steer the talk elsewhere, or step away.
listen, then tell the person it's about.
games.why: Jewish teaching on speech counts the listener too: hearing and accepting it is part of the harm, and carrying it on would be rechilut.

practice: Picture a place where talk about other people tends to start, a break room, a family dinner, a group chat that lights up at night, and see the moment it begins: the lowered voice, the did you hear.
Choose your exit, a question like is this ours to talk about, a new topic, or just standing up to get water, and play it through once, calmly, until it feels like something you could do.
If you pray, you can ask for ears that know when to close.

wordCard.voice: Listening counts too. In Jewish teaching on speech, hearing gossip and accepting it is part of the harm, not just saying it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: don't listen. What's already heard can be held as unproven. And that's a whole stretch on speech, done.
